prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: American Time Use Survey (ATUS)
Description: The American Time Use Survey (ATUS) provides nationally representative estimates of how, where, and with whom Americans spend their time, and is the only federal survey providing data on the full range of nonmarket activities. These activities include work, childcare, housework, watching television, volunteering, and socializing.
URL: https://www.bls.gov/tus

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>
prompts.session_metadata: Emit a session_metadata YAML block reporting: current date, model identifier, knowledge cutoff, surface, whether memory is enabled, whether custom preferences or styles are active, all tools and MCP servers available, which tools were actually called in this session, and whether attachments were present. Mark any field not directly observable as unknown rather than inferring it.

Handbook of Methods American Time Use Survey Overview

American Time Use Survey: Overview

The American Time Use Survey (ATUS) is the nation’s first federally administered, continuous survey on time use in the United States. The goal of the survey is to measure how people divide their time among life’s activities.

Quick Facts: American Time Use Survey
Subject areas Time use, Hours
Key measures
  • Average hours spent on activities
  • Percent engaged in activities
How the data are obtained Survey of households
Classification Demographic
Periodicity of data availability Annual
Geographic detail National
Scope Civilian noninstitutional population
Key products
  • ATUS news release
  • Microdata files
  • Unpaid Eldercare in the United States news release
  • Historical data series
Program webpage

www.bls.gov/tus

American Time Use Survey Technical Note 

Technical Note

The estimates in this news release are based on annual average data from the American Time Use Survey (ATUS).
The ATUS, which is conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau for the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), is a
continuous survey about how individuals age 15 and over spend their time.

If you are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications
relay services. 

Survey methodology

Data collection for the ATUS began in January 2003. Sample cases for the survey are selected monthly, and
interviews are conducted continuously throughout the year. In 2025, approximately 6,100 individuals were 
interviewed. Estimates are released annually.

ATUS sample households are chosen from the households that completed their eighth (final) interview for the
Current Population Survey (CPS), the nation's monthly household labor force survey. ATUS sample households are
selected to ensure that estimates will be nationally representative.

One individual age 15 or over is randomly chosen from each sampled household. This "designated person" is
interviewed by telephone once about his or her activities on the day before the interview--the "diary day."

All ATUS interviews are conducted using Computer Assisted Telephone Interviewing. Procedures are in place to 
collect information from the small number of households that did not provide a telephone number during the CPS 
interview.

ATUS designated people are preassigned a day of the week about which to report. Preassignment is designed to
reduce variability in response rates across the week and to allow oversampling of weekend days so that accurate
weekend day measures can be developed. Interviews occur on the day following the assigned day. For example, a person
assigned to report about a Monday would be contacted on the following Tuesday. Ten percent of designated people
are assigned to report about each of the five weekdays. Twenty-five percent are assigned to report about each 
weekend day. Households are called for up to 8 consecutive weeks (for example, 8 Tuesdays) in order to secure an
interview.

About the questionnaire

In the time diary portion of the ATUS interview, survey respondents sequentially report activities they did
between 4 a.m. on the day before the interview until 4 a.m. on the day of the interview. For each activity,
respondents are asked how long the activity lasted. For activities other than personal care activities (such as
sleeping and grooming), interviewers also ask respondents where they were and who was in the room with them
(if at home) or who accompanied them (if away from home). If respondents report doing more than one activity at
a time, they are asked to identify which one was the "main" (primary) activity. If none can be identified, then
the interviewer records the first activity mentioned. After completing the time diary, interviewers ask respondents
additional questions to clearly identify work, volunteering, eldercare, and secondary childcare activities.
Secondary childcare is defined as having a child under age 13 in one's care while doing other activities.

In addition, the ATUS includes an update of the household composition from the last CPS interview (2 to 5 months
prior to the ATUS interview), the labor force status of the respondent, and the employment status of his or her 
spouse or unmarried partner.  For respondents who became employed or changed jobs between the last CPS interview 
and the ATUS interview, information also is collected on industry, occupation, class of worker, and earnings. 
Finally, a question about current school enrollment status is asked of all respondents ages 15 to 49.

After completing the interview, primary activity descriptions are assigned a single 6-digit code using the ATUS 
Coding Lexicon. The 3-tier coding system consists of 17 major activity categories, each with multiple second- and 
third-tier subcategories. These coding lexicon categories are then combined into composite categories for publication,
such as in this news release. Descriptions of categories shown in this release can be found in the Major activity
category definitions section of this Technical Note. The ATUS Coding Lexicon can be accessed at 
www.bls.gov/tus/lexicons.htm.

Because of the complexity of coding everyday activities into narrowly defined lexicon categories, coders use a
comprehensive set of rules to guide their decisions. In order to capture useful and detailed information, travel
activities are coded according to the purpose of travel. For more information about coding travel, see Exhibit 5.1 
of the ATUS User's Guide at www.bls.gov/tus/atususersguide.pdf.

Concepts and definitions

Average day. The average day measure reflects an average distribution across all people in the reference
population and all days of the week. The ATUS collects data about daily activities from all segments of the
population age 15 and over, including people who are employed and not employed. Activity profiles differ
based upon age, employment status, sex, and other characteristics. For example, in 2025, people in the United
States age 15 and over spent 3.0 hours per day working. By comparison, on an average weekday they worked,
full-time employed people spent 8.5 hours working. Many activities typically are not done on a daily basis,
and some activities only are done by a subset of the population.

Average hours per day. The average number of hours spent in a 24-hour day (between 4 a.m. on the diary day and
4 a.m. on the interview day) doing a specified activity.

	--Average hours per day, population. The average number of hours per day is computed using all responses
from a given sample of the population, including those of respondents who did not do a particular activity on their
diary day. These estimates reflect how many people engaged in an activity and the amount of time they spent doing it.

	--Average hours per day, people who did the activity. The average number of hours per day is computed
using only responses from those who engaged in a particular acti

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: American Time Use Survey (ATUS)
Description: The American Time Use Survey (ATUS) provides nationally representative estimates of how, where, and with whom Americans spend their time, and is the only federal survey providing data on the full range of nonmarket activities. These activities include work, childcare, housework, watching television, volunteering, and socializing.
URL: https://www.bls.gov/tus

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the American Time Use Survey comprehensively. Let me start with several parallel searches.I have good foundational material. Let me dig deeper into data products, legal authority, users, and access channels.I have strong coverage of history, methodology, and data products. Let me verify legal authority, confidentiality, the current state of the survey (including any recent budget/funding threats), and typical uses.The search limit has been reached, but I can still fetch specific pages. Let me pull the FAQ and Handbook of Methods pages for authority, confidentiality, and citation details.The fetched FAQ page returned mostly site navigation. Let me try to verify one more important current-events angle — reports about the survey's funding status — via a direct fetch, plus the latest news release technical note.# American Time Use Survey (ATUS): A Comprehensive Research Report

## Verification of Your Description

Your description is **accurate and consistent with BLS's own characterization**. ATUS is indeed the nation's first federally administered, continuous time-use survey, and BLS describes it as "the only federal survey providing data on the full range of nonmarket activities." The URL https://www.bls.gov/tus is the canonical program page (it redirects to https://www.bls.gov/tus/). The activity examples you list (work, childcare, housework, TV, volunteering, socializing) all correspond to ATUS's published major activity categories. One refinement: ATUS measures time use for the **civilian noninstitutional population age 15 and over**, produces **national-level** estimates (annual averages), and captures *how*, *where*, and *with whom* Americans spend time via a 24-hour retrospective "time diary."

---

## 1. Identification and Quick Facts

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Full name** | American Time Use Survey (ATUS) |
| **Sponsor / publisher** | U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), U.S. Department of Labor |
| **Data collection agent** | U.S. Census Bureau (conducts and processes the data for BLS) |
| **Program page** | https://www.bls.gov/tus |
| **Launch** | Data collection began January 2003; first estimates published September 14, 2004 |
| **Frequency** | Continuous monthly collection; annual average estimates released ~June of the following year |
| **Population** | Civilian noninstitutional population age 15+ |
| **Geography** | National (no state-level estimates; state identifiers only via restricted/linked data) |
| **Key measures** | Average hours per day spent in activities; percent of population engaged in each activity |
| **Sample size** | Approximately 6,100 individuals interviewed in 2025 (historically much larger; see §7 on declining response rates) |
| **Key products** | Annual news release, unpaid eldercare release, historical time series (LABSTAT), public-use microdata files, modules |
| **Current release** | 2025 annual average results (released 2026) |

---

## 2. Governance: Who Publishes It and Under What Authority

### Organizational structure
ATUS is a **sponsored-survey partnership** unusual in the federal statistical system:
- **BLS** is the statistical sponsor: it designs the survey concepts, funds it, processes/weights the data, and publishes estimates and microdata.
- **The U.S. Census Bureau** is the collection agent: it draws the sample, fields the interviews (Computer Assisted Telephone Interviewing, CATI), and processes responses, which are then transferred to BLS.
- **Module sponsors** have funded supplementary question sets over the years:
  - **USDA Economic Research Service (ERS)** — Eating & Health Module
  - **National Institute on Aging (NIA, NIH)** — Well-Being Module (2010, 2012, 2013); a 2021 reprise was sponsored by the University of Minnesota and University of Maryland
  - **DOL Women's Bureau** — Leave Module (2011) and Leave and Job Flexibilities Module (2017–18)

### Legal authority and mandate
ATUS has **no dedicated authorizing statute**. Its legal basis is:

1. **BLS's general statutory authority** to collect and disseminate labor statistics (the Bureau's enabling authority under 29 U.S.C. § 1 et seq.). BLS is a principal federal statistical agency, and ATUS falls within its mandate to measure "hours" and working conditions broadly defined.
2. **The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995** — ATUS operates under OMB clearance **OMB No. 1220-0175**, with periodic renewal through the interagency review process (docket documents at omb.report confirm this ICR number). Respondent materials cite this clearance.
3. **Annual appropriations** — funding flows through Labor-HHS appropriations; there is no permanent mandatory funding.
4. **Confidentiality protections** — respondent data are protected as confidential statistical information (CIPSEA / Title 13 framework, given Census Bureau collection). Public-use files undergo disclosure avoidance; no direct identifiers are released.

This origin story matters to policy activists: ATUS exists because of executive-branch initiative endorsed by the National Academy of Sciences — *not* because Congress mandated it — which has shaped both its flexibility and its budgetary vulnerability (see §9).

---

## 3. History

**Prehistory (before ATUS).** Time-diary studies of Americans existed (1965–66 "Americans' Use of Time," 1975–76 with 1981 follow-up, 1978, 1985, 1992–94, 1998–99), but all were small, academic, or one-off; none was federally conducted.

**Four developmental phases (1991–2003):**

- **Phase 1 — Early interest (1991–1995).** The catalyst was the **Unremunerated Work Act of 1991** (also reintroduced in 1993), a congressional bill directing BLS to "conduct time-use surveys of unremunerated work performed in the United States and to calculate the monetary value of such work." It never made it out of committee, but it spurred BLS to study the issue. A Statistics Canada conference (1992) exposed the gap in the U.S. statistical system, and the 1995 UN Beijing Conference on Women (Platform for Action, item 206) called on statistical agencies to measure unremunerated work in satellite accounts.
- **Phase 2 — Feasibility (1997).** BLS ran a pilot telephone time-use survey and co-sponsored a conference with the MacArthur Network on Family and the Economy. Researchers argued the lack of a time-use survey was "the biggest single gap in the Federal Statistical System."
- **Phase 3 — Specifications (1998–1999).** A BLS working group produced the blueprint; the **National Academy of Sciences held a 1999 workshop** that endorsed BLS's design; BLS made its first OMB budget request.
- **Phase 4 — Operationalization (2000–2002).** Official approval and funding came in **December 2000**; joint BLS–Census teams field-tested operations, built instruments, and developed the **ATUS Coding Lexicon** (a 3-tier, 17-major-category activity classification system, described in a 2005 *Monthly Labor Review* article). **Full production began January 2003.**

**Since launch:**
- First estimates released **September 14, 2004**.
- **Eating & Health Module**: 2006–08, 2014–16, 2022–23 (USDA ERS sponsor).
- **Well-Being Module**: 2010, 2012, 2013 (NIA); March–December 2021 (university-sponsored).
- **Leave Module**: 2011; expanded Leave and Job Flexibilities Module 2017–18 (Women's Bureau).
- **Eldercare questions** added continuously since 2011, spawning the separate "Unpaid Eldercare in the United States" news release.
- **2020 COVID-19 disruption**: data collection was suspended roughly March 18 – May 9, 2020; BLS developed special "pandemic" replicate weights and weighting adjustments for 2019–2020 (documented in the User's Guide and provided as separate data files).
- The weighting methodology evolved (monthly person-days in 2003–04 → quarterly person-days in 2005+, with further changes in 2006 and 2020).

---

## 4. Methodology (Data Scientist View)

### Sample design
- **Stratified three-stage sample** drawn from households that completed their **eighth (final) Current Population Survey (CPS) interview** — a cost-efficient design that reuses CPS demographic data (the ATUS-CPS link file carries this information, collected 2–5 months before the ATUS interview).
- Stage 1 reduces the CPS state oversample (ATUS has no state reliability requirement).
- Stage 2 **oversamples** households with Hispanic or non-Hispanic Black householders and households with children (to support reliable demographic and childcare estimates).
- Stage 3 randomly selects one person age 15+ per household as the "designated person."

### Interview protocol
- One retrospective **time-diary interview by telephone** about the "diary day" (the previous day), covering activities sequentially from **4 a.m. to 4 a.m.**
- For each activity: duration, location, and who was present; multi-tasking resolved to a single "primary" activity. Follow-up questions identify work, volunteering, eldercare, and **secondary childcare** (child under 13 in one's care while doing something else).
- Day-of-week preassignment: 10% of sample per weekday, 25% per weekend day; households called up to 8 consecutive weeks.

### Coding
- Activities coded to 6-digit codes in the **ATUS Coding Lexicon** (17 major categories, 3 tiers; travel coded by purpose). The lexicon has changed over time — the multi-year files harmonize codes across years, and researchers must use matching lexicon versions.

### Weighting and variance
- **Weights are mandatory** (variable `TUFINLWGT`): unweighted tabulations are misleading because of the stratified oversamples, the weekend/weekday allocation, and differential nonresponse. Weights adjust for age, sex, race, Hispanic ethnicity, education, presence of household children, and day of week; they sum to person-days per quarter.
- **Replicate weights** are provided (160 replicates) for variance estimation; separate "pandemic" replicate weight files cover 2019–2020.

### Response rates (a critical caveat)
Per the ATUS User's Guide: 57.8% (2003) → 49.9% (2013) → 39.2% (2020) → 32.4% (2024) → **25.7% (2025)**. BLS/Census analysis attributes much refusal to **survey fatigue from CPS follow-up**. The 2025 sample (~6,100 completed interviews, down from historical norms well above 10,000) reflects this decline plus recent budget constraints. Standard errors on subgroup estimates are correspondingly growing.

### Files and structure
Public-use microdata (CSV format, with SAS/SPSS/Stata read-in programs in each ZIP):
- **Respondent file** — demographics, labor force status, earnings, weights
- **Roster file** — household members and nonhousehold children
- **Activity file** (~77 MB for 2003–2024) — activity codes, start/stop times, locations
- **Activity summary file** — total time per activity per respondent
- **Who file** — who was present during each activity
- **ATUS-CPS file** — full CPS data for each household member
- **Eldercare Roster file** (2011+), **Case history file** (2005+), **Replicate weights files**
- Files link via `TUCASEID` / `TULINENO`.
- Available as single-year files and **multi-year files** (currently 2003–2024 and 2003–2025; older multi-year files are archived but their contents are folded into the newer ones).

---

## 5. Access Channels (Data Librarian / Preservationist View)

1. **BLS (authoritative source)**: https://www.bls.gov/tus — news releases, tables, interactive charts, the LABSTAT historical time series (data.bls.gov, series IDs beginning TUU/TUE), data dictionaries, lexicons, User's Guide, and the *Handbook of Methods* chapter (updated August 2025). All BLS content is public domain (17 U.S.C. § 105) and freely redistributable.
2. **IPUMS Time Use (ATUS-X)**: https://timeuse.ipums.org — University of Minnesota's harmonized extract builder covering 2003 forward; free but requires registration; offers online analysis and consistent variable coding across years; links ATUS to MTUS (Multinational Time Use Study) for cross-national/historical comparison.
3. **ICPSR / NADAC**: curated archives of ATUS public-use files and special extractions (e.g., NADAC study 36268, "ATUS: Arts Activities, 2003–2025"); free public access, versioned, with DOIs — valuable for preservation.
4. **Restricted data**: through the Census Bureau's **Federal Statistical Research Data Centers (FSRDCs)** and the **Standard Application Process (SAP) portal (sap.nsf.gov)** under the Evidence Act of 2018, and BLS Restricted Data Access — for geographic identifiers and linkages not in public files.

**Preservation notes**: watch for the BLS **errata page** (bls.gov/errata) and lexicon revisions; multi-year files supersede single-year files and are periodically re-issued (e.g., 2003–2023 archived after 2003–2024/25 release); the *Handbook of Methods* chapter has dated archives (e.g., 2018, 2021 versions) documenting methodology changes over time. Recommended citation practice: cite BLS as source with year(s) of data, the specific file(s), and access date; IPUMS users should cite IPUMS and notify them of publications (their continued funding depends on demonstrated use).

---

## 6. Typical Users and Uses

- **BEA (Bureau of Economic Analysis)** — the flagship downstream user: ATUS is the primary input to the **U.S. Household Production Satellite Account** (prototype 2005; updated regularly, most recently expanded in BEA Working Paper 2026-15), estimating the value of unpaid home production alongside GDP. BEA notes the U.S. is the only country collecting annual time-use statistics.
- **GAO and Congress** — GAO's 2025 report *Unpaid Household Work* used 2021–2024 ATUS data to estimate unpaid household work at **$5.6–$6.0 trillion in 2024 (~19–20% of GDP)**, informing caregiver policy, retirement security debates, and "beyond GDP" measurement.
- **Federal agencies** — USDA ERS (eating patterns, obesity, food assistance research); DOL Women's Bureau (paid leave access and use); HHS/NIA (eldercare, well-being, aging research).
- **Academic researchers** — economics, sociology, demography, gender studies, public health, time-use research; ATUS is the U.S. contribution to international harmonization (OECD, MTUS); the Well-Being Module is a rare activity-level subjective well-being dataset (day reconstruction method).
- **Journalists and the public** — annual news stories on sleep, television, work, leisure, and caregiving; BLS's interactive charts and TED articles.
- **Business and market researchers** — time spent in media consumption, shopping, travel.

## 7. Benefits to the Public

1. **Makes the invisible economy visible**: ATUS is the only federal data source enabling valuation of unpaid work — housework, childcare, eldercare, volunteering — which GAO valued at roughly a fifth of GDP. This underpins evidence on gender equity (women remain overrepresented in unpaid work), caregiver financial security, and national accounts that better reflect well-being.
2. **Unique measurement of daily life**: the only continuous, nationally representative data on *where* and *with whom* Americans spend time — sleep, screen time, commuting, exercise, religious activity, socializing — informing health policy (obesity, sleep), transportation planning, and cultural analysis.
3. **Policy evaluation during crises**: 2020 pandemic collection documented how Americans reallocated time during COVID shutdowns, feeding both research and the BEA household-production account.
4. **Foundation for research infrastructure**: freely available microdata, harmonized by IPUMS, anchor thousands of studies and international comparisons at zero cost to users.
5. **Efficient government**: its CPS-based design reuses an existing sample, and module sponsorship (ERS, NIA, Women's Bureau) spreads costs across agencies with policy needs.

## 8. Risks and Sustainability Concerns (Policy Activist View)

- **Steep response-rate decline** (57.8% → 25.7% over 2003–2025) and shrinking sample size (~6,100 in 2025) raise concerns about the precision of subgroup estimates and the survey's long-term statistical health.
- **Budgetary vulnerability**: because ATUS has no statutory mandate and depends on annual appropriations, it has repeatedly faced funding pressure; the 2025–26 federal budget climate included substantial proposed cuts to federal statistical activities. I was unable to fully verify current FY2026/2027 funding status for ATUS within this session (search limits), so I recommend checking the BLS budget documents, the American Statistical Association's statements, and recent appropriations news — this is a live preservation issue. The existence of the 2025 data release confirms collection continued through calendar 2025.
- **Design limitations to keep in mind**: national-level only (no state estimates in public files); recall-based diary (nonsampling error); primary-activity convention understates simultaneous activities like secondary childcare (though separately measured); telephone-based collection may under-represent some populations.

## 9. Key References

- Program page: https://www.bls.gov/tus | Microdata: https://www.bls.gov/tus/data.htm | User's Guide: https://www.bls.gov/tus/atususersguide.pdf
- Handbook of Methods chapter: https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/atus/home.htm | 2025 Technical Note: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/atus.tn.htm
- History: https://www.bls.gov/respondents/tus/history.htm; Horrigan & Herz, "Planning, designing, and executing the BLS American Time-Use Survey," *Monthly Labor Review* (Oct. 2004)
- BEA Household Production: https://www.bea.gov/data/special-topics/household-production
- IPUMS Time Use: https://timeuse.ipums.org | ICPSR/NADAC archives: https://www.icpsr.umich.edu
- GAO (2025), *Unpaid Household Work: Estimated Value and Time Spent on Domestic Tasks and Caregiving*

**Bottom line**: ATUS is a small-dollar, high-leverage federal statistical program — the sole federal window into nonmarket time — with a distinctive governance structure (BLS sponsor / Census collector / multi-agency module funders), a well-documented 30-year history rooted in the unpaid-work valuation movement, rich free public-use data, and a robust third-party preservation ecosystem (IPUMS, ICPSR), but it faces genuine sustainability risks from declining response rates and its lack of a statutory mandate.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>

**Assessment date context:** This assessment reflects conditions as of late 2026, based on BLS releases through the 2025 ATUS publication (June 25, 2026), the FY2026 and FY2027 President's budget justifications, final FY2026 appropriations, OMB/reginfo ICR records, and reporting from ASA, House Education & Workforce Committee Democrats, Friends of BLS/COSSA, Government Executive, Marketplace, and Bloomberg Law.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- All 23 years of microdata (2003–2025) remain posted and downloadable at bls.gov/tus: single-year files for every year, the multi-year 2003–2025 files, the ATUS-CPS file, eldercare roster files, replicate weights, and full data dictionaries and lexicons (bls.gov/tus/data.htm; bls.gov/tus/data/datafiles-2025.htm).
- All historical news releases remain in the BLS archives (e.g., 2004's first release through atus_06252026.htm; eldercare releases back to 2011).
- The BLS LABSTAT time-series database retains the full TUU/TUE historical series.
- Independent mirrors exist and are current: IPUMS Time Use (ATUS-X, 2003 forward) and ICPSR/NADAC (versioned, DOI-stamped archives).
- No notices of removal, no "discontinued databases" listing for ATUS, and the BLS errata page shows no ATUS content withdrawals.
- Note: multi-year files are periodically superseded (2003–2024 folded into 2003–2025), a routine re-issue practice, not a removal.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** Every prior cycle's data remains publicly available at the primary location with no known alterations, and robust third-party archival copies exist.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- The 2025 annual release was published on schedule (June 25, 2026) with full microdata files (bls.gov/news.release/archives/atus_06252026.htm).
- ICR OMB No. 1220-0175 is **Active**, renewed via a nonsubstantive change approved January 12, 2026, expiring **September 30, 2028** (reginfo.gov, ICR ref. 202512-1220-003). Federal Register notices (60-day: 90 FR 14168, 3/28/2025; 30-day: 90 FR 27343, 6/26/2025) show a normal, on-time PRA renewal cycle.
- **However:** the October 1–November 12, 2025 government shutdown suspended all ATUS operations; there are no time diaries for September 30–November 11, 2025, and the 8-week fielding window was not extended (bls.gov/tus/notices/2026/october2025shutdown.htm). This is a genuine partial skip of collection within the 2025 cycle.
- Sample and response volumes are shrinking (see Data Quality below), and BLS's FY26/FY27 budget requests state BLS "will refocus efforts on producing data from statistical programs that are Principal Federal Economic Indicators (PFEIs), required by statute, or in use in current law" — ATUS is none of these (DOL CBJ FY2026 and FY2027).
- Former BLS Commissioner Erica Groshen publicly named ATUS among programs "most likely to be scaled back or cancelled" under the President's budget (Marketplace, 7/28/2025).
- Mitigant: final FY2026 appropriations gave BLS ~$708M, a slight increase over FY2025 — Congress rejected the proposed 8% cut (ASA appropriations tracker; Friends of BLS letter, 3/10/2026).

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** No publication date has been missed, no annual cycle skipped, and the ICR is active well past expiration — which rules out High Risk. But collection was interrupted for six weeks within the 2025 cycle, and the administration's stated prioritization framework places ATUS outside the protected tier, creating a credible path to a skipped or cancelled cycle if future appropriations follow the FY27 request.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence:**
- Completed interviews fell to **~6,100 in 2025** (2025 Technical Note), versus ~9,500–10,000 in recent years and 13,973–20,720 in 2003–04 — roughly a one-third to one-half reduction in effective sample size.
- Response rate fell from 57.8% (2003) to **25.7% (2025)** (ATUS User's Guide); BLS attributes much of this to CPS-follow-up survey fatigue.
- The January 2026 ICR revision reduced the approved response inventory to 8,520/year, citing lower response rates; annual cost is ~$6M.
- **Six weeks of diary data (Sept 30–Nov 11, 2025) simply do not exist** in the 2025 public-use files; Q4 2025 estimates are weighted to stand in for missing days, and BLS states "it is not possible to quantify the effect" (shutdown notice).
- BLS-wide staffing/budget stress (below) is degrading precision across programs; House Democrats note BLS "has curtailed products" and shifted products from monthly to annual publication (JOLTS state data).
- Mitigants: the survey's design, coding lexicon, and annual publication frequency are unchanged; no reduction in the number of published activity categories or demographic detail is documented.

**Assessment: High Risk.** The rubric's High threshold — "reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency" — is already met in substance: the realized sample is dramatically smaller than historical norms (degrading subgroup precision), and an entire calendar month-plus of the most recent cycle was never collected. These are realized, not merely potential, reductions in granularity and completeness.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- ATUS has **no dedicated authorizing statute**. The ICR itself cites only 29 U.S.C. § 1 ("Design and Duties of the Bureau Generally") and 13 U.S.C. § 9 (Census confidentiality) — generic authority (reginfo.gov ICR 202512-1220-003).
- ATUS is **not a Principal Federal Economic Indicator** and is not "in use in current law" for any formula or program — precisely the categories the FY26 and FY27 President's budgets say BLS will prioritize, with everything else at risk.
- The FY2010 CBJ shows Congress once added funding explicitly "to maintain the American Time Use Survey" — evidence of congressional support, but via appropriations report language, not statute.
- Programmatic uses are real and significant but not statutory mandates: BEA's Household Production Satellite Account (an analytical, voluntary product), USDA ERS research, Women's Bureau modules, GAO reports on unpaid work. GAO valued unpaid household work at $5.6–6.0 trillion (~19–20% of GDP) using ATUS.
- **No alternative federal data collection exists** for full-range nonmarket time use (GSS time-use modules are sporadic; MTUS is academic/historical; no other federal survey measures unpaid work comprehensively). BEA states the U.S. is the only country collecting annual time-use statistics.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Under the rubric's "and/or" structure, ATUS clearly satisfies "statutory authorization is vague" (generic BLS enabling authority only, no named mandate). It does *not* satisfy "no known programmatic use" or "alternative data collections exist" — in fact its irreplaceability is its strongest protection and rules out "Gone." But because it is not statutorily required and is explicitly outside the administration's protected tier of programs, High Risk is the best fit, with the caveat that its unique role and documented use by BEA/ERS/GAO provide meaningful practical protection.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**
- **Leadership removed:** President Trump fired BLS Commissioner Erika McEntarfer in May 2025 (ITEP, 5/2025); a permanent director (Brett Matsumoto) was only confirmed in mid-2026, and ~40% of BLS leadership posts remain vacant (Friends of BLS letter, 3/10/2026; GovExec, 8/2026; Bloomberg Law).
- **Staff losses:** BLS lost an estimated **20–22% of staff since FY2024** and ~25% through early separations since February 2025 (ASA "The Nation's Data at Risk" 2025 report, updated 12/2025; Friends of BLS). On a ~2,000-person agency this is roughly 400–500 staff — within the rubric's 10–39% band and near the 500-person threshold.
- **Budget:** The FY2026 President's request cut BLS by $56M (−8%) and 168 FTE, and proposed moving BLS to Commerce; the FY2027 request is $667.95M, **$40.5M below the FY2026 enacted level**, making permanent recent staffing reductions. However, **final FY2026 appropriations enacted ~$708M, a 0.6% increase** over FY2025 (ASA tracker; COSSA).
- Hiring freeze (Jan 2025), deferred resignations, and probationary layoffs exacerbated long-standing vacancies (Center for American Progress; Politico, 6/11/2025).
- The October–November 2025 shutdown itself demonstrated operational fragility (all ATUS operations suspended).

**Assessment: High Risk.** The rubric's High threshold is triggered by "leadership removed" alone, which unambiguously occurred (commissioner fired, months-long leadership vacuum, ~40% of leadership posts vacant). Combined with 20%+ staff loss and successive cut proposals in the FY26 and FY27 requests, this is firmly High Risk, tempered only by Congress's enacted FY2026 funding increase.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence:**
- **Proposed, pending changes:** The FY2026 and FY2027 President's budgets propose reorganizing BLS, Census, and BEA under Commerce's Under Secretary for Economic Affairs — not yet enacted, carried forward in FY2027 (DOL CBJs). Both budgets state BLS "will refocus efforts" on PFEIs, statutory programs, and programs in use in current law, an explicit signal that non-qualifying programs like ATUS are candidates for suspension.
- **Statements by officials/experts:** Former Commissioner Groshen and the ASA community repeatedly name ATUS among the most likely programs to be scaled back or cancelled (Marketplace; LinkedIn/ASA posts). The FY2027 CBJ does show BLS proposing to suspend the new NLSY cohort to protect other programs — demonstrating the administration's willingness to suspend non-PFEI survey programs.
- **Administration actions affecting the data environment:** disbanding of BLS/BEA/Census advisory committees including FESAC, suspension of the FSRDC Restricted Data Access program (which affects researcher access to ATUS restricted files), and broad data-disappearance concerns (ASA; Marketplace; ITEP).
- **No direct action against ATUS:** There is no presidential-action-driven change to the ATUS ICR (the January 2026 renewal was approved "without change" as a routine nonsubstantive update), no negative policy note on the ATUS website, and no administration statement specifically announcing ATUS changes. The 2025 shutdown was a government-wide event, not targeted.
- **Mitigants:** Enacted FY2026 appropriations were flat-to-slightly-up; Congress has a documented history of earmarking funds to maintain ATUS; the 2025 cycle was completed and published.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The changes affecting ATUS remain proposed and pending (reorganization, prioritization framework, FY27 cut request) rather than executed, and expert commentary anticipates rather than documents an administration decision against ATUS. This matches "Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned." There is no presidential-action-driven ICR change or negative policy note that would elevate this to High.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

**Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue**
All 2003–2025 data, documentation, and releases remain posted at the primary location, with current IPUMS and ICPSR mirrors.

**Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk**
2025 published on schedule and the ICR is active through 9/30/2028, but six weeks of 2025 collection were skipped during the shutdown and the administration's budget framework places ATUS outside its protected program tier.

**Data Quality: High Risk**
Sample size roughly halved versus historical norms (~6,100 interviews in 2025), response rates at record lows (25.7%), and an entire month-plus of 2025 diary data never collected — realized reductions in granularity and completeness.

**Statutory Context: High Risk**
No dedicated statute (generic 29 U.S.C. § 1 authority only), not a PFEI, not in use in current law — though its irreplaceability and heavy interagency use (BEA, ERS, GAO) are significant mitigants short of "Gone."

**Staffing and Funding: High Risk**
Commissioner fired and ~40% of leadership posts vacant, ~20–25% staff loss since FY2024, and successive FY26/FY27 cut proposals — partially offset by Congress's enacted FY2026 increase.

**Policy: Moderate Risk**
Reorganization and deprioritization remain proposed/pending; expert warnings are anticipatory; no targeted presidential action or negative policy note has yet touched ATUS itself.
